name: Apollo 16
first: First Moon landing in the lunar highlands — Descartes; John Young's "lunar Grand Prix"
description: The fifth crewed Moon landing and the first to a non-mare highland site. Geologists had expected Descartes to be volcanic; Apollo 16 disproved this — every rock returned was breccia (impact-shattered debris), reshaping understanding of the lunar highlands as products of catastrophic impacts rather than ancient volcanism. Young and Duke completed three LRV-supported EVAs totalling 20 h 14 m, traversed 26.7 km, and returned 95.7 kg of samples (the heaviest Apollo haul to that date). Young's "lunar Grand Prix" — a televised speed test of the LRV — peaked at ~17 km/h. Duke's 11-second hop attempt during a long-jump record attempt put him at risk of damaging his PLSS backpack and was called off. Charlie Duke's family photo + the "Far-UV Camera/Spectrograph" — the first astronomical observatory operated from the surface of another world — both ended up at the landing site. Mattingly, originally on Apollo 13 (replaced before launch over German measles concerns), finally got to fly to the Moon.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Saturn V (AS-511) from Kennedy Space Center LC-39A 1972-04-16 17:54 UTC.

events.label: SPS ANOMALY
events.note: Pre-descent: a backup SPS gimbal oscillation forced a 6-hour landing-vs-abort engineering review in real time. Landing ultimately approved.

events.label: TOUCHDOWN
events.note: Orion lands at Descartes Highlands 1972-04-21 02:23 UTC — first highland (non-mare) landing.

events.label: FIRST HIGHLANDS EVA
events.note: EVA-1: ALSEP deployment + LRV deployment + first scientific traverse of the lunar highlands.

events.label: LUNAR GRAND PRIX
events.note: EVA-2: Young's televised LRV speed test ("lunar Grand Prix") — peak speed ~17 km/h. Geology traverse up Stone Mountain.

events.label: FAR-UV CAMERA
events.note: EVA-3: First astronomical observatory deployed on the surface of another world (NRL UV camera-spectrograph).

events.label: ASCENT
events.note: Orion lifts off after 71 h 02 m on surface. 95.7 kg samples returned — heaviest Apollo haul to that date.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: CM splashed down in Central Pacific 1972-04-27 19:45 UTC. Recovery by USS Ticonderoga.
